title: The Dyer Who Invented Chemical Warfare Treaties
event_summary: In August 1675, France and the Holy Roman Empire signed the Strasbourg Agreement, the first known international treaty banning the use of chemical weapons — specifically poison bullets and projectiles filled with toxic compounds. The agreement arose after French and German forces had deployed belladonna-laced musket balls and arsenic smoke devices in border skirmishes, causing agonizing deaths that horrified even hardened soldiers. A local Strasbourg dye-maker named Johann Kunckel, who had supplied chemical compounds to military arsenals and witnessed the gruesome results firsthand, petitioned both sides' commanders to outlaw such munitions, providing detailed testimony about the poisons' effects.
why_forgotten: The treaty was overshadowed by the broader Franco-Dutch War and Louis XIV's territorial ambitions, which dominated diplomatic histories. Kunckel himself became better remembered for his later glassmaking innovations, and his role in chemical weapons diplomacy was buried in municipal archives. Nineteenth-century historians writing about the laws of war focused almost exclusively on the later Hague Conventions, treating earlier efforts as irrelevant proto-agreements.
why_it_matters: The Strasbourg Agreement of 1675 established the foundational legal principle that certain weapons are too inhumane for warfare — a concept that directly informed the 1899 Hague Declaration, the 1925 Geneva Protocol, and ultimately the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention that governs global policy today. Without this precedent, the idea that sovereign nations could mutually agree to ban entire categories of weapons technology might have taken far longer to develop. Every modern debate about banning autonomous weapons, cluster munitions, or biological agents traces its legal DNA back to this obscure Franco-Imperial accord.
